subject: Re: Packly performance handback — tokenframe & capacity clarification

Subject: Packly performance handback — tokenframe & capacity clarification

Hi Evan / Maya — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and the asks we captured so the team can size a short pilot and validate SLOs. Please correct anything I missed.

Summary of what we heard
- Primary use: interactive customer support flows (chat + context) with occasional multi-document lookups.
- Expected user concurrency: 150–300 active sessions during peak business hours (US-Eastern).
- Typical session traffic: 6–12 messages per session, median message ~180 tokens, high tail messages up to ~1,200 tokens (document extracts).
- Streaming: yes — Packly will stream tokens to the client for low-latency typing experience.
- Latency target: 95th percentile round-trip (inference only) target <= 350 ms for streaming-first flows; non-streaming completion endpoints can accept up to 700 ms p95.

Quantities we asked for (requested on call) — please confirm the numbers you actually observed in the attached snapshot or call out if these are estimates:
1) Sustained baseline QPS (messages/sec) during a regular business hour window
2) Peak crest QPS and how long crest typically lasts (seconds/minutes)
3) Token ingress rate aggregated (tokens/sec) at baseline and crest
4) Average and 95th percentile output length per message (tokens)
5) Fraction of requests that require streaming vs single response

Immediate asks / next steps
- Evan to send the workload snapshot CSV (schema in attachment) — we agreed on a trimmed export with 7 days of real traffic.
- Redwood to propose a pilot capacity mapping (slot sizing + stream concurrency knobs) and a short SLO validation plan.
- Hold a 30-minute ops sync (internal + Packly ops) once the CSV is ingested; propose times below.

Attachments: packly_workload_snapshot.csv (you mentioned you would share), sample pilot plan (we’ll attach a first draft after we ingest), and our SLO handbook excerpt for streaming recommendations.

Proposed times for ops sync (PST/EST windows): Tue 11/16 09:00 PST / 12:00 EST or Wed 11/17 11:00 PST / 14:00 EST. Let me know which works.

Thanks — Marissa

Thanks Marissa — attaching the 7-day trimmed export as discussed (attached as packly_workload_snapshot.csv). Past week is a representative window; here are the clarifications from our side:

Snapshot highlights (actual observed numbers)
- Baseline concurrent active sessions: 110–140 (we see a gradual ramp from 08:00–11:00 EST).
- Peak concurrent sessions (crest): up to 420 for short bursts during promotional events (typical crest duration: 90–180 seconds).
- Baseline message QPS (per second, aggregated): 28–34 qps.
- Peak crest QPS: sustained 130 qps for ~2 minutes in the event window; short spikes to ~190 qps lasting 10–30s.
- Token ingress (baseline): ~5.5k tokens/sec aggregated.
- Token ingress (peak crest): ~22k tokens/sec aggregated.
- Avg output length: 95 tokens; p95 output length: 420 tokens.
- Streaming fraction: ~62% of requests use streaming output (typing UX); the remainder are short, single-shot completions.

Additional notes
- We route heavy document-extraction requests to a background worker; these are out of the streaming path but do occasionally contribute to token ingress peaks.
- We can instrument per-route tags if Redwood needs to separate streaming vs non-streaming traffic in the pilot.

Attached: packly_workload_snapshot.csv (export), small export notes.

Let us know which pilot slot you recommend and the target SLOs you will validate. Tue 11/16 09:00 PST is tight for us; Wed 11/17 11:00 PST would be ideal.

—Evan

Subject: Re: Packly performance handback — tokenframe & capacity clarification

Evan — thanks for the numbers, that CSV was very helpful. Quick read and a proposed sizing approach for the pilot / SLO validation.

What we mapped from your snapshot
- Baseline sizing target: design for 40 qps sustained with headroom (we’ll provision to cover baseline + 25% buffer). This maps to ~6k tokens/sec baseline after accounting for average output.
- Crest handling: design for concurrent short burst capacity to handle 130 qps sustained for 2 minutes with autoscale policies to absorb spikes to 190 qps.
- Streaming concurrency: because ~62% of traffic streams, we recommend reserving dedicated streaming slots to isolate prefix KV residency (reduces tail latency). For pilot we propose 20 streaming slots with per-slot concurrent stream limit = 20 sessions.

SLO targets (pilot validation)
- Streaming path: inference p95 <= 350 ms (inference-only), p99 <= 650 ms under baseline; during crest we’ll monitor drop in p95 but aim to keep degradation within +50% bound.
- Non-streaming path: inference p95 <= 700 ms, p99 <= 1.2s.
- Error rate target (5xx + timeouts): <0.5% baseline, <2% during crest.

Pilot plan (high level)
1) Ingest CSV and wire per-route labels (streaming vs non-streaming) — Redwood ops (Neha) to validate ingestion and produce traffic generator config.
2) Run a 2-hour steady-state run (40 qps) and capture p50/p95/p99, then run a crest window test: 3 cycles of 2 minutes at 130 qps with 30s spikes to 190 qps.
3) Validate caching and KV residency behavior for streaming slots and measure memory footprint.
4) Deliver a short pilot report with recommended slot counts and autoscale thresholds.

Ops asks for Packly before pilot
- Confirm whether you can enable per-route tags in your export (streaming=true / false) — that will let us re-create exact mix.
- Share any throttling rules or client-side rate-limits we should simulate.
- Confirm whether promotional crest windows are predictable (scheduled) so we can schedule load tests to mirror them.

Scheduling: Wed 11/17 11:00 PST works for us. Neha, can you own ingest + initial generator config? Jonas — can you stand by for the crest experiments?

Thanks — Karthik
